passage: Dear Osei, the model railway is out of the attic. I write this sentence first because you will want to sit down for the rest: your father, who swore the layout would stay boxed until retirement, has annexed the entire spare room, and I have signed the treaty because the alternative was the dining room. Thirty-one years those boxes waited, and everything works except what does not: the green locomotive, the one you saved your paper round money for, ran on the first try, while the station clock, the signals, and your father's temper all needed new springs. He has joined a club that meets Wednesdays above the ironmongers, twelve men and one alarming teenager who knows everything, and they speak a language of gradients and couplings that I have stopped pretending to follow. The plan, pinned to the wall like a battle map, shows the village from my childhood window: the mill, the level crossing, the church without its spire, as it was before the lightning of 1959, a detail he researched at the county archive for an entire rainy week. He is happier than I have seen him since the foundry closed. Send him the photographs of the harbor branch you took in the spring; he pretends not to ask. Come at Christmas and bring the boys; trains, I am assured, are inherited. Your loving mother, Dorthe.
question: On which day does the railway club meet?

passage: Dear Ms. Fairweather, I am returning, with this letter, the library's copy of The Shepherd's Calendar, borrowed, the slip informs me, on the 4th of March, 1987, by my late father, Gregor Anholt, and found last month behind the water tank in his loft, where it had evidently fallen from the shelf above and been given up for lost. The fine, calculated at your current rate, would come to something over 2,700 dollars, and I have consulted the family and we feel strongly that we should pay it, not as penance but as gratitude, because the book did not spend those decades idle: my father, unable to return what he could not find, bought a second copy, and it was that guilty replacement he read to us on winter nights, so that the poems in it are, for three of his children, the sound of his voice. If the library's rules cap the fine at some smaller figure, as I suspect they must, I ask that you accept the balance as a donation to the children's section, in his name, spent on whatever is currently falling apart from love, which he would consider the only respectable condition for a book. The water damage to the top corner predates the loft, I am afraid; he read in the bath. Yours sincerely, Nadia Anholt.
question: Where was the missing library book found?

passage: Dear Tam, herewith the promised report on your bees, from your deputy, who reminds you that she volunteered for two weeks and is now in week five, a fact the bees and I discuss often. All three hives flew well through the warm spell. The white hive is the strong one, as you said, and wants a second super before you are home or there will be comb in the roof again; I have put it on, actually, this Tuesday gone, because your instructions said use judgment, and my judgment was that waiting for your permission by postcard was how the roof comb happened in July. The garden hive threw a swarm on the 9th despite everything, settled, considerately, on the plum at head height, and is now the property of young Pieter from the mill lane, who took it in a borrowed box with his veil on backward and his mother watching from the car with the windows up; he has named the queen, which I understand is not procedure, but he guards them like a dragon and reads to them from a bee book on Sundays, so they have landed well. Stores look thin in the middle hive; I fed syrup, two to one, twice. Nothing stung me until I said aloud it had been a month of nothing; you may draw conclusions. Come home before the ivy flow. Yours, Runa.
question: Who took the swarm that settled on the plum tree?

passage: Dear Mr. and Mrs. Castellane, my name is Ivo Brandt, and I believe your house was my grandmother's; she was Liese Brandt, and she lived at what was then number 5, the house with the two chestnuts, from her marriage in 1932 until the family left in the hard spring of 1946. She died in February at a great age, and among her papers we found a plan of the garden, drawn in her own hand and dated the week they left, showing what was planted where: the asparagus bed against the south wall, the row of currants along the wash house, and, marked with a circle and the word for the youngest, a walnut tree planted the autumn her last child was born. I write, plainly, to ask whether the walnut stands. She never asked anyone to check, in the way of people who cannot afford the answer, but she spoke of it the last time we walked in her nursing home garden, wondering aloud whether anyone was eating the nuts or whether they lay in the grass for the squirrels, which, she wanted it known, she considered an acceptable outcome. If it stands, a photograph would make five Brandts very happy. If it does not, please do not soften it; we are a family that prefers the plain answer. With respect, Ivo Brandt.
question: What word did the grandmother write beside the circled walnut tree on her plan?

passage: Dear Solveig, the choir tour is over, we are home, hoarse and insufferable, and you, who missed it for the wedding, will now receive the account you dreaded. Four towns in six days by coach, 41 singers, one conductor, and Mrs. Prendergast's famous hamper, which fed the altos exclusively by a system no one dares question. The first two concerts went as rehearsed, which is to say well, with the church at Elmsford so full they opened the vestry doors and sat the overflow among the bell ropes. The disaster and the miracle both came at Rathvale: the organ failed entirely ten minutes before we began, some ancient fuse beyond the verger's arts, and Maestro, after one long look at the ceiling, had us sing the whole program unaccompanied, including the Wexler mass, which we have never once rehearsed without organ, and I tell you, Solveig, in the silence where the organ should have entered in the Gloria, forty-one people breathed together like one animal and went on, and the basses, the basses of all people, held the pitch to the end, dropping barely a quarter tone across the whole mass, which Maestro announced from the podium afterward the way generals announce victories. Grown men from the town wept openly. We took eleven minutes of applause. The organ, repaired next morning, was almost resented. Practice is Tuesday; you have scales to do. Love, Astrid.
question: In which town did the organ fail before the concert?

passage: Dear Nephew, since you ask what I think of the offer, and since your mother will give you the soft version, here is the hard one, with love. Take the apprenticeship. The university will still exist in four years; the last master cooper in the county is 71 and will not. I have known Espen Dahl since we were boys, and he has never taken an apprentice before, not once, though he has been asked by better connected families than ours; he watched you at the fair repairing that split churn lid with a butter knife and a tantrum, and he saw what I have seen since you were small, that your hands think. The wage is poor, 1,400 a month against your friend Milo's software money, and the first year is sweeping, steam, and sore thumbs, and he will bark at you in that way that sent the last three inquirers home by Friday. Bark back once, politely, in the first month; he is testing for spine, not obedience. What you will have at the end is a trade nine people alive can still do properly, a bench that is yours, and work that will outlast every program Milo writes, some barrels going easily fifty years in service. Your grandfather made the pact with his hands and never regretted it; neither have I; the vote in this family runs three generations deep. Decide by the equinox, as Dahl asked. Uncle Stellan.
question: How old is the last master cooper in the county?

passage: Dear Pia, the results of the great kitchen experiment, as demanded, before you commit your own savings to the same madness. The verdict first: worth it, narrowly. The builders came in March promising three weeks and left in June, and the difference, I want this in writing for your planning, was not idleness but the wall: the moment they opened it, we found the chimney breast resting on a lintel of, and I quote the structural engineer's report, timber, hope, and paint, and everything stopped for sixteen days while a steel beam was ordered, at 1,900 dollars nobody had budgeted, and inspected twice. Budget accordingly: whatever your quote says, keep a fifth again behind your back and mention it to no builder. The happy part: the room is transformed, the morning light reaches the table as the architect promised, drawn in pencil on the plans with a little sun and an arrow that I thought was decoration and was in fact the whole point, and the drawer for the baking trays, which I fought for against three separate professionals who called it wasted space, is the single most praised object in the house. Cook in the room in your head for a month before you sign anything; that drawer came from imaginary Sunday baking, and it beats everything the catalogue suggested. Come and see it at Easter. Floury love, Greta.
question: How much did the unbudgeted steel beam cost?

passage: Dear Emmerich, I have found the field notebooks, and the story of where deserves telling before the notebooks themselves reach you, which they will by registered post next week, insured, wrapped, and, I confess, photographed page by page first, trust in the postal service having limits. When the institute cleared grandfather's office in 1988, the botany department kept his herbarium sheets but the notebooks, all nineteen of them, were listed as returned to family, and the family, as you know, has spent thirty years denying receipt in every direction. They were in the piano stool. Aunt Vilma's piano stool, the one nobody may sit on, which came from his study, and which she defended from sale, from woodworm treatment, and from two house moves with a ferocity we all misread as sentiment about the piano. Whether she knew, we will never settle; she was capable of both the knowing and the forgetting. They are in beautiful order: the mountain seasons of 1949 through 1967, every specimen numbered in his brown ink, and, folded into the last one, a letter to whoever finds this, which I have not opened, because it says on the front, in his hand, to be read aloud, all of us together. Christmas, then, and no arguments. Bring the good schnapps. Your cousin, Leni.
question: Where were the field notebooks found?

passage: Dear Coach Brandvold, you will not remember me, and that is rather the point of this letter. I swam in your Tuesday and Thursday junior lanes at the old Corporation baths from 1979 to 1984, one grade forever behind the medal winners, and I write because of something you did that you will certainly have forgotten. At the district trials in my last year, I false started twice and was out, thirteen years old and crying into a towel behind the filter house, and you came and sat on the wet tiles in your good trousers and said nothing for a while, and then you said, the water does not remember, and went back to your medal winners. I have carried that sentence for forty years. I said it to myself at my first driving test, at two funerals, and in the corridor outside the interview for the job I have now, headmistress of a school of 300 children, where I have said it to more crying thirteen-year-olds than I can count, always sitting down beside them first, because the sitting, I understood eventually, was the larger half of the sentence. My granddaughter starts in your club's junior lanes in September, third generation. The baths are new, the lanes are the same. Some debts one simply reports. With enduring thanks, Margarethe Voss.
question: What sentence did the coach say behind the filter house?

passage: Dear Board of the Kelsey Lane Housing Cooperative, this letter resigns my seat on the garden committee, and since eleven years of service have earned me one letter nobody will enjoy, here it is. I resign over the lime tree. The vote on Tuesday to fell it was carried 5 to 4 on the argument of leaves in the gutters, and I sat in that room and heard a tree of 140 years, by the ring count of its own lost limb after the 2015 storm, weighed against a gutter cleaning bill of 300 dollars a year and found wanting by one vote. I have cleaned those gutters myself nine autumns of the eleven. The tree shades the south flats that cannot afford awnings, holds the corner soil that moved in the wet winter, and hosts the bees from Mrs. Okonkwo's hive that pollinate every garden plot we are so proud of in the newsletter; none of this appeared in the meeting's arithmetic. I know a lost vote when I lose one, and I will not chain myself to anything; I resign so that I may oppose the felling as a resident, with a resident's freedoms, beginning with the appeal to the borough tree officer filed this morning, of which copy attached. The committee keeps the shed key; the tree, with any justice, keeps the corner. Formerly yours, Hedvig Larsen, flat 9.
question: By what margin was the vote to fell the lime tree carried?
